# DECOMPILE

user asks for a file to decompile

ai harness reads the file and picks an abstraction shape from the kind of file.
it uses [the decompile skill](compiler/cli/human/skills/decompile/SKILL.md) and [the shape abstraction catalog](compiler/cli/human/shapes/README.md):
  [the rail](compiler/cli/human/shapes/rail.md) if one run.
  [the sections](compiler/cli/human/shapes/sections.md) if a set of functions.
  [the desk](compiler/cli/human/shapes/desk.md) if dispatcher.
  [the dialogue](compiler/cli/human/shapes/dialogue.md) if a rulebook.
ai harness writes the abstraction for [a reader who does not read code](compiler/cli/human/skills/decompile/SKILL.md:e1:explain), with pins on the words that name an entity. every other word is free.
ai harness shows the abstraction text and always stop. even if the user message sounded like approval.

user [says the word: map it.](e3:the word)

ai harness pipes the exact text into the [human map command using the CLI](compiler/cli/human/cmd_map.py:e1:cmd_map).
the cli verifies the new abstraction and it makes no claude call:
  [it checks the pins point at real code or files](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py:e1:build_anchors),
  checks no two pins share their words, [so there are no circular dependencies](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py:e1:check_cycle),
  check each block pin gets [its exact lines](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py:e1:block_spans).
  a refusal returns the error to the ai harness, which reads it, fixes the text, and runs again.
  words the user wrote himself go in with --verbatim: plain, kept as they are.
    [if a pin in them it refuses](compiler/cli/human/cmd_map.py:e1:verbatim_record) because the pins come after, with the [retext command](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py:e1:cmd_retext);
  a copy of them the verbatim stays in the json. called the ["origin"](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py:e1:origin_of), so a later mending can be measured against it.
cli creates one new abstaction appended to human/explanation_<path>.json, never updates
  
ai harness [reports](compiler/cli/human/skills/decompile/SKILL.md:e1:report): 
  the entry, its pins, the coverage,
  the warnings as if [human show](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py:e1:cmd_show) was run
  and offer the next abstraction to map:
    a zoom on one block, a file abstraction over the whole, or [the project itself](compiler/cli/human/cmd_project.py:e1:cmd_map_project)

# COMPILE

user gives an abstraction

ai harness follows [the human skill](compiler/cli/human/skills/human/SKILL.md): 
  [the run](compiler/cli/human/skills/human/SKILL.md:e1:the run)
  registers the project first, and your words reach the tool before any code is written.
  
cli, [human init](compiler/cli/human/__init__.py:e1:the register) registers the project:
  [sweeps the tree](compiler/cli/human/__init__.py:e1:the sweep) through [the ignore sieve](compiler/cli/human/__init__.py:e1:the sieve), 
  writes the file list into human/human.json,
  gives the project an id there once, which the training store knows it by,
  copies the reader in, and starts the empty project map.
  
ai harness hands your words to the project map as they are — human map project --verbatim — no spelling fixed, no word trimmed. 
[the verbatim gate](compiler/cli/human/__init__.py:e1:the guard) refuses a pin in them: 
  the pins come later, when the things they point at exist. 
  the entry is flagged as yours and keeps that first copy as its origin.
ai harness writes the code files, no comments. the gate is static like a compiler's: the file must parse.
ai harness maps the detailed abstraction:
   if for a file — entry 1, a catalog shape, pins into the blocks.
   if a human file, [an abstraction over many files with no code of its own](compiler/cli/human/helpers.py:e1:name_to_map), its pins reach files, blocks, abstractions of a file's map, and abstractions of the project map or of another human file.

[cli refuses a circle over the maps](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py:e1:check_cycle) so the pins run one way, down.

ai harness hands your words back with the pins inserted, through a plain retext of that entry:
 [the gate strips the pins out](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py:e1:the gate on your words) and compares the rest with the words it holds, character for character.
 a changed word is a refusal. 
 pins go in; your words never change on this road.

user rewords them later: 
  human retext project <id> --verbatim takes new words, resets the origin, and marks stale the entries that stood on the old words;
  a sync rewords them only when the code forces it, and says so.

ai harness reports, serves, and arms the watch, so what you write in the reader reaches it — flow 8.

afterwards user can correct with retext, undo, sync — the commands of flow 1.


# READ

user or ai harness runs: human serve, to start the reader from anywhere in the project:

cli climbs to the folder that holds human/human.json and [serves it](compiler/cli/human/__init__.py:e1:the shelf),
           printing the localhost line, [the tailnet line](compiler/cli/human/__init__.py:e1:tailnet address), the line that says
           an open training session shows as a layer over the reader, the line that says a new file
           from the reader lands next to the others, and the line
           that says a writing in the reader lands in human/server/ — flow 8.
cli answers human.json with [a live file list](compiler/cli/human/__init__.py:e1:rebuilt) — a fresh sweep on every ask,
           so a deleted file leaves the tree and a new one appears, no init, no restart.

user opens [the reader](compiler/cli/human/reader/web.html): 
  project.json opens first.
  a file shows [every abstraction as one folded header](compiler/cli/human/reader/web.html:e1:render), the higher layer first;
  a click on a pin [jumps to its abstraction](compiler/cli/human/reader/web.html:e1:jump) or it [switches files](compiler/cli/human/reader/web.html:e1:crossJump) 
  a click on project or human file pin lands on the abstraction and lights the anchor.


# SYNCRONIZATION

user changes the code
user or ai harness run human sync <name>
  
cli runs [a deterministic pass](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py:e1:cmd_sync):
  [maps every old line to its new line](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py:e1:the line map),
  [re-resolves every pin and every span](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py:e1:the re-resolving).
  if only lines moved, return.
cli finds the abstractions the change touches: lines changed, a pin broken, new lines inside the block.
cli writes instruction to ai compiler: 
  the file and its absolute path — read the whole file —, 
  the diff,
  [the project files it imports](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py:e1:the line about the neighbours),
  the blocks,
  the abstractions to mend,
  the rules:
    keep the untouched lines, 
    keep every anchor, 
    add a sentence for each behaviour the change added.
    an abstraction of your own words goes in [named as yours](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py:e1:the mark on your words),
    find the smallest edit, in the user's voice.

ai compiler [answers with the mended texts](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py:e1:ask_claude), 
runs at the project root,
the instruction given through the pipe and never on the command line, so a long one is not cut short.

cli [gates the answer on a copy](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py:e1:the rebuild), 
tries up to --tries times. checks if: 
  every block exists,
  every anchor kept, 
  every needed word alive. 
  four failures leave the map untouched.
  
the map gets saved; 
the abstractions that point into a mended one get marked stale:
  in the file's map,
  in every map with no code under it, when one of its abstractions pins the mended one if a word changed, and not if the pins alone moved.
           
shows warning:
  if [new lines landed inside an entry](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py:e1:the pieces the new lines fall in) and no word changed.
  if [the sync moved words of your own](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py:e1:the word when your words moved):
the first copy stays in the map, human show marks the entry with [the line that brings them back](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py:e1:the word about your words).

if user wants to sync the whole project or a human file, [human sync <bare name>](compiler/cli/human/cmd_project.py:e1:cmd_sync). which uses the old state: git HEAD;

cli asks git for [the files that changed](compiler/cli/human/cmd_project.py:e1:changed_files),
re-resolves the file, block, and abstraction pins,
[sends one instruction](compiler/cli/human/cmd_project.py:e1:cmd_sync) for the abstraction that pin a changed file.
           
a project abstraction with the user words goes in named as the users' there too.
the same warning follows when the answer moved them.


# A PARENT ABSTRACTION CHANGED

if abstraction 1 changed by a sync or a retext and a second abstraction points into it:
  abstraction 2 gets [marked as stale](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py:e1:mark_children) and a copy of the old text gets added to its json file.
           
the mark is a list. a second changed parent adds [a note of its own](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py:e1:add_note),
if parent changes twice before the repair then keeps its first old text. the versions between are the base of nothing. 
if abstraction 2 retexts it still keeps the mark; 
only if repair the mark gets off. which lets the tool know the mending happened and was not guessed.

user asks for the repair: human sync <name> --stale 2

cli writes the second letter: one page for each changed parent.
  its old text, 
  its new text, 
  the diff between the two
  then the dependent's text,
  the rules: mend the words that went wrong, 
  keep every anchor and [every word another entry needs](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py:e1:needed_words),
  carry a new fact down at the dependent's own level, pinned at the parent's new anchor.
if the dependent holds the user's words, the letter asks for the smallest edit, in the user's voice.
a parent that is gone stops the run.

ai harness answers with the mended dependent. words only, never code.

cli [gates and saves](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py:e1:repair_stale); 
marks the dependents of entry 2 as stale in turn.
a repair that moved words of your own is named on the spot, as a sync's is.
a parent's child can be a parent: the next abstraction layer waits for the users next word, one layer at a time. the layers cross maps too. a human file can be the parent of a human file. the chain never turns back on itself.
a project entry made stale by a file's entry is repaired the same way, each note naming the map and the abstraction it waits on, with the parent read from that map: [human sync project --stale](compiler/cli/human/cmd_project.py:e1:repair_stale).


# TRAIN

user gives this machine its key once: human login <key> — [the sessions live in a store](compiler/cli/human/__init__.py:e1:the store hand)
           away from your disk, and without the key the training refuses and says to log in.
           A session belongs to you and to one project, named by the id human init wrote into human/human.json;
           a project with no id is refused until human init runs.

user opens a session: human train --open. [Rows without a pick carry over](compiler/cli/human/cmd_train.py:e1:carry).
           A write in the reader that asks claude for a telling — a decompile, a create, an expansion
           with no words — [opens one by itself](compiler/cli/human/cmd_watch.py:e1:the training of an ask) when none is open.

ai harness, on the next /decompile or sync, or the next such ask of the reader, writes two or three versions per file instead of one:
           best — the catalog shape, with --shape; refinement — for a sync row only, the map's own text,
           filled by the tool, and refused on a new telling, which holds best and free and shows two
           cards in the layer; free — no shape rule. [Each version goes in with its own call](compiler/cli/human/cmd_train.py:e1:cmd_add),
           passes the same pin gates as a map — [the anchors the project map pins into the entry](compiler/cli/human/cmd_train.py:e1:the anchors the project map pins into it)
           among the ones it must keep — and a rewrite keeps its earlier text in the history.
           Each call answers with [the slots filled](compiler/cli/human/cmd_train.py:e1:the slots filled) and,
           on its own line, [the slots still empty](compiler/cli/human/cmd_train.py:e1:the slots still empty), so
           claude writes the missing one before it reports to you.
           An expansion goes in with the entry it hangs from and the highlighted words, one row for each
           such entry, and its versions may not pin into that entry.

cli keeps an open row current when the abstraction it studies is retexted, in a file's map, in the project map, or in a human file by you or by a sync: a row is a photo of its abstraction, and[the row follows](compiler/cli/human/cmd_train.py:e1:refresh_row) with a second photo.
           the copy of the entry's text it keeps becomes the new words, and a middle card that
           still held the old text takes the new one and keeps the old as v1. A middle already
           rewritten stays as it is, and the layer stops calling it current. A store that does not
           answer only warns here: the retext itself stands.

cli serves [the feed](compiler/cli/human/reader/web.html:e1:loadTrain) as a layer over the reader: an open session covers the page
           on its own, hide puts it away, a line in the bar with the counts brings it back, and so does a new row.
           The session list — from the store, this project's sessions only — and the fresh map come as JSON;
           [a pick lands in the open session](compiler/cli/human/cmd_train.py:e1:pick) over POST, no restart;
           a session of another project is not found.

user swipes and pick — sideways for the versions, up for the next row — and leave a comment if you want.
user closes: human train --close, or the close training button of the layer, which first says what the close will do.
  
cli gives a new telling with no pick [a version of its own](compiler/cli/human/cmd_train.py:e1:takes a version of its own) — best, or free
           when best is missing — and marks the pick as a default, so a write from the reader always lands.
           A sync row with no pick, or a row that misses its versions, is named and carries over.
  
cli [applies each pick](compiler/cli/human/cmd_train.py:e1:apply_row) as a retext of the entry or a new map, then [marks the session finished](compiler/cli/human/cmd_train.py:e1:cmd_close).
the maps never change before the close.
a pick that rewords an abstraction that a map with no code under it points at leaves a stale note there, one for each changed parent. 
when an expansion lands, [a link event](compiler/cli/human/cmd_train.py:e1:the pin of its target into the new entry) waits for the ai harness, so the highlighted words of the entry it hangs from are pinned down into it.
  
the training stores one session record under your name and the project's id, never a file on your disk: 
  the rows, 
  the versions with their shape and history, 
  the pick, 
  the comment, 
  and copy of the code or, for a map with no code under it, [of every file](compiler/cli/human/cmd_project.py:e1:snapshot) under it.


# EDITOR ON READER

user clicks the text of an entry: a box opens in its place, the raw text, pins and all. the same text retext takes — with the caret where you clicked, and it grows as you type.
a file with no map shows one place for its telling and the code of the file under it, and the bar says there is no abstraction yet; 
an empty map with no code under it offers a new abstraction, and once a map holds an entry that place is gone. 
escape, or a click away, closes the box and keeps what you wrote — only the box now open answers a click away;
a click on a pin jumps and opens no box. 
a pin you just typed, one the map does not hold yet, [is read from the target it names](compiler/cli/human/reader/web.html:e1:guessAnchor).
a pin the page cannot follow shows that target beside the words, and the caret counts past the shown name, so a click after such a pin still lands where you clicked.
typing keeps nothing: Ctrl+S puts the draft in the browser, and the bar says unsaved until you press it.
your words [stay in the place you wrote them](compiler/cli/human/reader/web.html:e1:keepBox) when the page draws again between one box and the next.
the page keeps its place through all of it: the box opens, grows and closes where you were reading, and an empty place for a telling lights under the pointer, so you see it can be written in.

user makes a file from the page.
if new file line:
  at the top of the file tree it takes a path from the root, folders and all
  [the server makes the file empty](compiler/cli/human/__init__.py:e1:the new file), so it opens on its new abstraction.
  the code comes under your words. 
if human file:
  [the new human file over the tree takes a bare name](compiler/cli/human/__init__.py:e2:the human file).
  refuse if bare name is already held by another human file or a file at the root
  the map opens on its new abstraction with no file under it.
no event is queued.
a path out of the project, into human/, or onto a file already there is refused, with the reason. 
the tree follows the files on disk.
git holds no old copy of a file made here,so its first sync runs against an empty old version.

user asks for an abstraction the user did not write himself, by three roads: on a file with no map the open
           place carries a decompile button — not on an empty file, whose words come first — and one
           click asks claude for the whole-file telling;
           on a mapped entry you highlight words and right-click for expand abstraction, which opens a
           write place on top whose head is the button — your words there, or none at all; a right-click
           on the head of an entry gives create abstraction, a plainer telling over that entry, nothing
           to write. These three send themselves at the click and wait for no compile button, and each
           opens from [the little menu of a right click](compiler/cli/human/reader/web.html:e1:the menu).
           An expansion is a deeper telling of the words you highlighted: it stands above the entry,
           and the entry pins those words down into it, as a zoom on one block stands above the
           telling of the whole file.
user takes an abstraction away: the same right-click on its head offers delete abstraction, and
           [the head turns into the button](compiler/cli/human/reader/web.html:e1:to take that one away), with a cancel beside it.
           One click takes the entry out at once — this road waits for no compile button and queues
           no event, because nothing is left for claude to do.
  
cli, it runs human undo <name> --entry <id>, and [the gate refuses it](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py:e1:the gate)
           while another entry, the project map, or an open training row still stands on that entry.
           [The open row comes over the network](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py:e1:the training store): a machine with
           no key goes through without that last look, and a store that does not answer, or a project with no id, stops the undo.
  
user presses the compile button, which stands in the bar while a text differs from the map:
           [it sends every place you changed](compiler/cli/human/reader/web.html:e1:compile), one after the other. The map changes only then.
  
cli takes the writing at the door — [its body read as JSON](compiler/cli/human/__init__.py:e1:the body) —
           and [runs the command you would have typed](compiler/cli/human/cmd_watch.py:e1:the command run), one per changed text:
           an entry rewritten goes in as human retext <name> <id> --verbatim, a first telling as
           human map <name> --verbatim, and code on a file with no map is written to the file.
           An expansion you wrote words for goes in the same way, as human map <name> --verbatim, so the
           map holds your words before claude works; an expansion with no words, a decompile and a
           create map nothing at the click — the event alone waits. On a machine with a key and a store
           that answers, that event names the open training session, one opened for it when none was — flow 6.
           A file under human/ is refused — the maps take no writing.
           The gates are the ones of flow 1: a refusal comes back to the page in the command's own
           words, named by the place it came from, and nothing is queued.

one event appended to human/server/events.jsonl: the kind, the name, the paths of the map and
           the file, the entry, the old text and the new, and for a code write
           [the pins that reach the file](compiler/cli/human/cmd_watch.py:e1:the pins that reach a file).
           An expansion and a create name the entry they stand on, and an expansion carries the
           highlighted words with their pins.

user arms the listening once, from the project root: human watch.

cli [prints every event claude has not finished](compiler/cli/human/cmd_watch.py:e1:cmd_watch), one JSON line each, then
           follows the queue; --once prints what waits now and returns. An event printed in an earlier
           session comes back marked replay, so claude reads the maps before it syncs anything.

ai harness takes them in order, by [the writing part of the human skill](compiler/cli/human/skills/human/SKILL.md:e1:the writing):
           reads the diff of your words, writes the code they ask for — in a new file when no file of the
           project holds that thing —, syncs every map that stood on
           them, and pins the new sentences back in. A decompile, a create, or an expansion with no
           words has no text of yours to read: claude writes that telling itself and maps it — or, when
           the event names a training session, writes it twice into a row, maps nothing, and the close
           of flow 6 maps your pick. A link event from that close asks only for the last step of an
           expansion: the highlighted words of the entry pinned down into the new one.
           Then [human ack <number>](compiler/cli/human/cmd_watch.py:e1:cmd_ack) — the queue
           advances and says how many are left.

user sees the wait in the page: the entry is marked compiling until the ack, because the reader
           [asks every three seconds](compiler/cli/human/reader/web.html:e1:pollQueue) and the door answers with
           [what still waits](compiler/cli/human/cmd_watch.py:e1:pending). When the wait ends, the page reads
           that map again, so the new words show, and the training looks again for new rows.

  find [the row of this name](same_row) for the same abstraction, or the same block and target, or makes it.
  refuses when what the row is about changed since the row was made — the file's text, or for a map with no code under it [the copy the project run keeps](compiler/cli/human/cmd_project.py:snapshot).
  
  It refuses --as refinement on a create row, whose two versions are best and
  free; the middle slot is a sync row's.
  It checks the text and makes it the version of that slot — with the shape it
  follows and the moment — and sends the session back to the store.
  A slot written twice keeps the new text on top and the old one in its history.
  It says the row number, the kind, the level, the entry, the entry it expands,
  the shape, the pins, [the slots filled](slots_of), [the slots still empty](empty_slots), how
  many earlier texts a rewrite keeps, and the session the row went to.

[new_row](new_row)(a, root, file_path, name, data, src)
    file_path is the file on disk, none for a map with no code under it; 
    name is its path from the root, or the bare name of that map; 
    data is its map; 
    src is its text, or the copy project run keeps.
    a row is one file's turn in a session: which file, what the picked text will
    do to its map, a copy of the code, the three versions, and the pick.
    the level says where the picked text lands. 
    the tool reads it from what you typed: --kind sync takes the entry given, or the whole-file one, and lands on
    "same" — the text replaces that entry's text; --entry lands on "same" too;
    --block lands on "above" — a new zoom on one block, refused for a map with no code under it, which has no blocks of its own and is named in the refusal; neither is "first" on an empty map — the
    first entry of the file — else "below" — a plainer layer under the whole-file entry.
    --target makes the row an expansion: it names the entry the new text hangs
    from, and --words gives the words highlighted in that entry. It goes with
    --block or alone, never on a "same" row; it needs the words, and the entry
    must be in the map.
    The row it makes holds the file, the kind, [the path of the map](map_rel), the
    entry, the level, the block, the target and its words, a copy of the old text,
    a copy of the code, three empty slots, no pick, no comment, not applied, and the times.
    A sync row gets the old text into its middle slot, as a version with no shape.

[whole_file_entry](whole_file_entry)(data, code_name)
    The tool finds the lowest abstraction whose block is the file itself or the name of the map, when map has no code under it.
    It exists only so a sync row without --entry knows which entry it refines.

[check_text](check_text)(text, row, data, spans, root)
    text is one version; spans are the blocks of the file with their lines.
    The tool checks the pins as the map would: every pin names a real block or
    a real earlier entry, a text that replaces an entry keeps the pins other
    entries depend on, and no circle forms. A text that replaces any entry
    also keeps [the anchors the project map pins into it](compiler/cli/human/cmd_project.py:pins_into),
    so a version cannot break the map of the whole project, or the map of a human file.
    An expansion may not pin into the entry it hangs from: that entry pins down
    into the expansion at the close, so a pin up would make a circle.
    
  a row on a map with no code under it is checked the map's way, so a pin into a file, into an abstraction of a file's map, into a map with no code under it, or into an abstraction of map with no code under it, passes.
  the circle check of such a row follows the pins from one map into the next, so a circle that runs through two maps is caught too.
  a failed check stops with the reason.
  this is why a picked text can always be applied later.

[pick](pick)(root, sid, row, slot, comment)
    The feed sends sid, the session id in its address; row, the row's place in
    the list from 0; slot, the version you picked, or none to take a pick back;
    and comment, your reason, or none.
    Outside the lock the tool refuses a slot it does not know and a comment that
    is not text. Under the lock it asks the store for the session and hands a
    refusal of the store back as it came — no such session, no key on this
    machine — while a store that does not answer becomes 502. Then it refuses a
    session of another project with 404, a finished session, a row it does not have, the refinement of a create row —
    which holds best and free only — and an empty slot; then it writes
    the pick, the comment, and the time and sends the session back, and a refusal
    or a silence on that write is answered the same way.
    It gives back a status and the row, or a status and the error text.

[refresh_row](refresh_row)(root, code_name, eid, old_text, new_text)
    code_name is the file, or the word "project"; eid is the entry a retext just
    rewrote; old_text and new_text are its words before and after.
    A row is a photo of its entry, taken when the row is made. This is the
    second photo. [The retext of a file](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py:cmd_retext)
    and [the retext of the project](compiler/cli/human/cmd_project.py:cmd_retext)
    call it, so an open session never trains against words that are gone.
    Nothing happens when the words did not change, when this machine has no key
    for the store, or when no session is open. A store that refuses or does not
    answer only prints a warning; the retext itself stands.
    The tool takes the row about that entry — not yet applied, landing on "same" —
    and leaves it alone when its picked version already says the new text: that
    is the close applying the pick.
    Otherwise the row's copy of the old text becomes the new text. When the
    middle slot still holds the old text untouched, it takes the new text too
    and keeps the old one as v1; a middle already rewritten by hand stays, and
    the feed stops calling it "current". The tool says which row followed and how.

[cmd_close](cmd_close)(root)
    You type `human train --close`. The tool runs [the close](close) and prints
    what it says; a close that fails stops the command with that text. Otherwise
    it names the user the session went to the store under.

[close](close)(root, said)
    said is the list the tool writes what it did into.
    Under the lock the tool needs an open session; with none it gives back 404.
    It takes the rows not yet applied in order, "below" rows last, so a plainer
    layer finds the entry it points at. A create row with no pick
    [takes a version of its own](default_slot) and is marked as defaulted. A row
    still with no pick is named with the versions it misses, and it carries over.
    When what a row is about changed since the row was made, the tool marks the
    row and says so. It applies each row; on a failure it remembers the row and goes on.
    When an expansion row is applied, [the pin of its target into the new entry](link_event)
    waits for claude as an event, and the tool says the event's number.
    Any failure leaves the session open, names the rows, and gives back 409. With
    none, the tool marks the session finished, says the counts, says that the rows
    without a pick carry over, and gives back 200 with all it said.

[close_road](close_road)(root, sid)
    The feed's close: sid is the session id in its address.
    The tool refuses with 409 when that is not the open session of this project, then runs
    [the same close as the command line](close). A refusal of the store comes back as it came; a store
    that does not answer becomes 502. It gives back what the close said and
    whether the session finished, or a status and the error text.

[apply_row](apply_row)(root, row)
    the tool takes the latest abstraction of the picked version.
    a "same" row retexts its abstraction and gives the abstraction's id back;
    a row of map with no code under it goes to the cmd_project.py logic flow retext, on the map of that name.
    any other row maps a new entry, with the block for a zoom — into the map with no code under it — and gives the new id back.
    The close writes that id into the row, so the row and the map can be joined later.

[link_event](link_event)(root, row, eid)
    eid is the entry the expansion became.
    The tool writes a "link" event into [the queue of the watch](compiler/cli/human/cmd_watch.py:append_event)
    — the map, the file, the target, its highlighted words, and the new entry —
    so claude pins those words of the target down into the expansion.
    It gives back the number of the event.

[run_with_text](run_with_text)(fn, text, ...)
    fn is the old command, map or retext; text is the picked version.
    The tool writes the text to a scratch file, calls the command with it,
    and removes the file. It exists only so a picked text reaches the old
    commands the way a typed text would.

[cmd_train](cmd_train)(a)
    The door. --open and --close allow no file and find the project from
    where you stand. A hand-in needs a file and finds the project from the file;
    a hand-in of the word "project", or of a human file by its bare name, finds it from where you stand.
    Whichever run it calls, a store that refuses — no key, no such session — or
    does not answer stops the command in this one place, with that reason.
    A project whose human/human.json holds no id stops here the same way, and
    the reason says to run `human init` once at the root.

[the map run](compiler/cli/human/cmd_map.py), [the tool](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py), [the training desk](compiler/cli/human/cmd_train.py) and [the name reader](compiler/cli/human/helpers.py)

WORD
project — the word you type where a file path goes: human map project, human show project, human sync project
a human file takes its bare name the same way: human map <name>

CROSS_RE
the look of a pin into another map: the name, a colon, e and the entry number, a colon, the anchor words.
the name is a file's path, the word project or a human file's name. the form is the same. only the reading of the name changes.

SYNC_PROMPT
the letter to claude when the project changed: read the changed files, mend the words the change made wrong, add a sentence for each behaviour the change added, keep every pin, and give an entry of the user's own words the smallest edit in the user's voice


human/project.json is an abstraction of the whole codebase. a human file json is an abstraction of multiple files or folders.
both have no code of its own.
both have pins which reach: 
  other files,
  one block of a file
  one anchor of a file's abstraction
  another project or human file abstraction

every run below takes [the name you gave](name_of) — project, or a human file's bare name — and works on that map.

[cmd_map_project](cmd_map_project)(abstraction_name)
    the abstraction name is what you typed after human map project, or after human map <name> for a
    human file: the text on stdin, --verbatim when
    the words are yours, and no --block, because the map has no blocks of its own; the refusal names
    the map you gave.
    The tool checks every pin, refuses a circle — in this map or through another one — and appends
    one entry. It prints how
    many pins reach files, entries of other maps, and earlier entries of this map — and
    how many files of the project have a pin.
    With --verbatim the words must come in plain — a pin is refused, because the pins
    come after, with retext — and a copy stays beside the entry as the origin.

[build_anchors](build_anchors)(abstraction_text, data, self_id, root)
    abstraction text is the abstraction being mapped.
    data is the map it goes into; self_id is the entry's own number.
    The tool walks the pins of the text one by one. A pin whose target reads like
    app/main.py:e1:the start is [a pin into another map](cross_anchor);
    every other pin — a file, a block of a file, an earlier abstraction of this map — goes to
    [the shared pin checker](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py:build_anchors) one at a time.
    Two pins with the same words are refused here, because the shared checker sees
    only one pin at a time.

[cross_anchor](cross_anchor)(words, name, eid, aw, project_root)
    name is what the pin points at; 
    eid is the entry number; 
    aw is the anchor words.
    call name_to_map(name, project_root) and get the map path and its sort type.
    if name sort type file. then it must be a file of the project.
    if name sort type project or human file. there's no file to check.
    
    the tool refuses the pin when:
      the name has no map
      the map has no such abstraction
      when the abstraction has no anchor with those words.

    a good pin is stored with the name, the abstraction, and the anchor words, so the reader can walk from this abstraction to that abstraction, and to the anchors inside it.

[cmd_retext](cmd_retext)(a)
    a is the entry number, the new text, and --verbatim when the words are yours.
    The tool replaces the text of one entry of the named map the way it does for a file: the pins
    the other entries of this map point at must survive, the pins another no-code map holds into
    this entry must survive too, and no circle may appear.
    The words are the text without its pins. When the words changed, the entries of this map
    that point into this one are marked stale, and the entries of the other no-code maps that
    point into it are marked stale in turn, each named with its map; a retext that only moves the
    pins says so
    and marks nobody. An entry that holds your own words refuses a change of those words;
    --verbatim lets the change through and keeps the new text as the origin, or puts the
    flag on an entry that had none. A stale mark the new text did not answer stays, and
    the tool names the repair. Last, the row of the open training session that studies
    this entry [takes a second photo](compiler/cli/human/cmd_train.py:refresh_row) of it,
    so the feed shows the words the map holds now and keeps the old ones as v1.

[cmd_undo](cmd_undo)(a)
    a is the entry number, or nothing for the last entry of the named map.
    The tool removes that entry — unless another entry of this map points into it, unless another
    no-code map points into it, or the open
    training session holds a row on it that is not applied yet.

[cmd_show](cmd_show)(a)
    The tool prints every entry of the named map with its pin count, a stale mark that names every
    file's entry and every earlier entry that changed, and, for an entry of your own words,
    that it holds them — and whether they were reworded since they were mapped, with the
    way to bring them back among the warnings. Then the other warnings: a pin whose file is
    gone, whose name — the project or a human file — has no map, whose block is gone, whose entry
    or anchor in another map is gone
    ([the cross check](check_cross)), whose stored lines are old; each names the map to sync. Last,
    [the coverage](print_coverage): the files of the project that have a pin, out of all of
    them, and the names of the files without one.


the three doors the file maps knock on

[pins_into](pins_into)(root, code_name, eid)
    The anchor words of entry eid of the file code_name that the no-code maps — the project map and
    every human file, code_name's own map apart — point at.
    A retext, a sync, a stale repair, or a training version of that entry adds these to
    the words it must keep. Empty when no such map exists.

[maps_into](maps_into)(root, code_name, eid)
    The names of the no-code maps that point into entry eid of code_name. An undo of that entry is
    refused while the list is not empty, and the refusal names the map to retext first.

[mark_stale](mark_stale)(root, code_name, eid, old_text)
    The tool adds a note to every entry that points into entry eid of code_name — in the project map
    and in every human file, code_name's own map apart — with
    the file, the entry, and the old text, and gives back the map name and the entry number of each.
    The file's
    retext, sync, and stale repair call it after the words changed, so the telling above
    knows a fact under it moved; a retext, a sync, and a stale repair of a no-code map call it the
    same way, so a human file that pins the project map, or the other way about, hears the change
    too. The note joins the ones the entry already holds, one per
    parent; a parent already noted keeps its first old text, so a second change does not
    hide the first.


the project changed

[cmd_sync](cmd_sync)(a)
    The old state of the project is git HEAD, so --old is refused. With --stale the tool
    goes to [the stale repair](repair_stale) instead.

    ●  the tool asks git what moved                        ([the files that changed](changed_files))
    │     The files the project knows — listed or pinned — that git sees
    │     changed, added, or gone, against HEAD.
    │
    ●  the tool takes a second look at every pin           ([the second look](re_resolve))
    │     File pins, block pins, and pins into other maps — a pin into a
    │     human file is looked at as soon as that map is there, because it
    │     has no file of its own; a gone target
    │     is broken. The candidates are the entries that pin a changed
    │     file, plus the entries with a broken pin. With no candidate the
    │     map is saved — no claude call.
    │
    ●  the tool writes the letter
    │     The root, the changed files with their full paths, [their diff](project_diff),
    │     [the broken pins](broken_note) — each with the anchors its entry
    │     holds now, so a reworded anchor can be retargeted —, the files of
    │     the project, the candidate texts — each named as your own words
    │     when it holds them —, and the words other entries need.
    │
    ●  claude answers, the tool checks                     ([the asking](ask))
    │     Up to --tries times. Each answer is [rebuilt on a copy](rebuild) and
    │     refused when a pin is dead, a needed anchor is gone, or an entry
    │     that is not a candidate was rewritten; the refusal goes back to
    │     claude with its name.
    │
    ●  the map is saved
          The changed texts are reported line by line, with a warning for
          every entry of your own words the answer changed. The entries that
          point into a changed one are marked stale — when the words changed,
          not when the pins alone moved — in this map, and in the other
          no-code maps that point into it, each named with its map.

[repair_stale](repair_stale)(a, root, data, name)
    ●  the tool gathers every parent the notes name
    │     An entry of a file's map when a note names a file, an earlier
    │     entry of this map otherwise. A parent that is gone stops the run.
    │
    ●  the tool writes the second letter
    │     The shared stale letter of [the file repair](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py:repair_stale),
    │     one page per parent — its old text, its new text, the diff between
    │     them, and the form a pin at it takes: file, entry, and anchor words
    │     when the parent lives in a file; entry and anchor words otherwise.
    │     An entry of your own words adds one rule: the smallest edit, in
    │     your voice.
    │
    ●  claude answers, the tool checks
    │     The answer must keep the words other entries need — those of this
    │     map and those another no-code map pins at this entry — and make no
    │     circle, up to --tries times.
    │
    ●  the map is saved
          The mended text replaces the old one, every note goes, and the
          entries that point into this one are marked stale in turn — in this
          map, and in the other no-code maps, each named with its map —
          when the words changed. A repair that moved your own words is
          named on the spot.

[snapshot](snapshot)(root, kind, name)
    What a training row keeps of the named map: for a new telling, a copy of every file
    [under that map](files_under); for a sync row, the files under it that changed, their copies,
    and their diff. The row
    refuses a new version when this changed since the row was made.

finding the pieces of a file

[block_spans](block_spans)(path, lines)
    path is the file on disk; lines is its text, one line each.
    The tool finds every named piece of the file and the lines it covers, so a
    pin can only point at a real piece. A markdown file gives its headings, a web
    page its once-only tags and its functions, a python file its functions and
    classes — read by python's own reader of code. Any other file has no pieces.

[md_spans](md_spans)(path, lines)
    Every heading is a piece that runs to the next heading of the same or a
    higher level. Headings inside a code fence do not count. Two headings with
    the same words stop the run, because a name must point at one place.

[html_spans](html_spans)(path, lines)
    The pieces of a web page, from two hands: [the once-only tags](tag_spans) — a
    tag that opens once, from its opening line to its closing line — and the named
    functions inside every script ([the script regions](script_regions) says where
    the scripts are). A function with the name of a tag stops the run.

[js_spans](js_spans)(path, lines, regions)
    regions are the line ranges of the scripts.
    The tool walks each script, notes where a function starts, and counts the
    braces line by line ([the brace count](brace_delta), which skips braces inside
    quotes and after //) to know where it ends. A function named twice stops the run.


checking the pins of a text

[build_anchors](build_anchors)(text, data, spans, self_id, folder)
    text is one abstraction; data is the map of the file; spans are its pieces;
    self_id is the entry the text belongs to; folder is the project root.
    The tool takes the pins one by one. The words must be there and appear once
    in the text. A pin into the code goes to [the resolving](resolve_code_target);
    a pin into an earlier abstraction must name an entry that exists, an anchor it
    holds, and never its own entry. It gives back the list of checked pins, each
    with its lines. One bad pin stops with the reason.

[parse_target](parse_target)(raw)
    raw is what stands in the parentheses of a pin.
    `e3:the start` is a pin into entry 3's anchor; anything else names a piece
    or a file.

[resolve_code_target](resolve_code_target)(words, raw, spans, folder)
    a piece of this file wins first. 
    then `file:piece` which is a piece of another file of the project. 
    then a file of the project on its own. 
    then a human file on its own, by its bare name
    anything else stops.

[check_cycle](check_cycle)(data, self_id, anchors, root, name)
    The tool follows the pins into earlier abstractions, and theirs, and stops
    when the chain comes back to the entry itself. A telling may not stand on
    itself. With a root and a map name it also steps into the maps the pins
    name ([the map behind a name](load_named_map)), so a chain that leaves this
    map and comes back is caught too.

  │     the text goes to the tool exactly as shown, through the pipe, with the name of the
  │     file and, for a zoom, the name of the piece it tells. The name can also be a telling
  │     with no code under it — the word project, or the bare name of a human file, which is
  │     made on the first word — and the text goes to that map instead; a name that carries a

  │     It opens the code and notes every named piece with its first and its last line.
  │     It does this for one reason: so a pin on a piece can be given its exact lines.

  │     no pin may make a circle back to the story it stands in. The circle is looked for
  │     through every map a pin reaches, so a chain that runs out to another map and comes

    │     file that is gone, or points at an anchor that is gone. For a
    │     python file it reads [the imported names](import_names) — plain
    │     imports and the `from .` ones of the same folder — and warns when
    │     a mapped neighbour has no pin in the whole-file entry. For the
    │     project it adds [the doubled lines](dup_warnings): a line of thirty
    │     letters or more that stands in the maps of two files, compared with
    │     pins and punctuation stripped ([the bare line](norm_dup)).
    │
    ●  the tool counts
          How much of the file is covered, and which lines are not.

[cmd_lines](cmd_lines)(a)
    The file with a number in front of every line.

[cmd_sync](cmd_sync)(a)
    You type `human sync file`, or `--old copy.py` when the last version does
    not live in git, or `--stale 3` to mend one dependent entry.

    ●  the tool sees what the change touched
    │     For the project map it only re-resolves the file pins and reports
    │     the gone ones. For a file that did not change it re-resolves the
    │     cross-file pins and stops. Otherwise it holds [the old lines](old_lines_of)
    │     next to the new ones and sees where each line went ([the line map](line_map)).
    │
    ●  the tool names the candidates
    │     Every entry whose lines ([the lines of an entry](entry_lines_set))
    │     the change touched, plus every entry whose piece is gone. An entry
    │     the tool may not reword ([the reword test](rewordable)) — the
    │     whole-file entry with no pin into the code — leaves the list,
    │     unless its piece is gone.
    │
    ●  the tool carries every entry and pin to its new lines    ([the re-resolving](re_resolve))
    │     With [the refresh of a file pin](refresh_file_anchor) for pins into
    │     other files; a pin at a map with no code under it stands while that
    │     map is on disk and is named gone when it is not. With no candidate
    │     it saves and stops — no claude call.
    │
    ●  the tool writes the letter
    │     The diff, the path of the file to read whole,
    │     [the line about the neighbours](touched_note) the file imports, the
    │     pieces, the candidate texts — each named as your own words when
    │     they are ([the mark on your words](verbatim_mark)) —, and the anchors
    │     they must keep.
    │
    ●  claude answers, the tool checks                    ([the rebuild](rebuild_all))
    │     Up to --tries times. Each answer is tried on a copy of the map:
    │     renamed pieces, new texts, every pin checked, every anchor another
    │     entry or the project map needs kept. One broken rule goes back to
    │     claude with its name.
    │
    ●  the map is saved
          The entries that point into a changed one — in this map and in
          every map with no code under it — are marked stale, when the words
          changed and not the pins alone. A text of your own words that the
          sync reworded gets a warning that names it
          ([the word when your words moved](warn_reworded)).
          A candidate that got new lines but kept all its words gets a warning
          that names [the pieces the new lines fall in](blocks_of).

[repair_stale](repair_stale)(a, code_path, root, map_path, data, lines, spans)
    ●  the tool gathers the parents
    │     One stale entry, and for every explanation it waits on the old text,
    │     the new text and the diff between the two ([the page of one
    │     parent](parent_note)); a parent that is gone stops the run.
    │
    ●  the tool writes the second letter
    │     The pages, the dependent's text, and the anchors it must keep — the
    │     pins of the maps with no code under them among them. An entry that
    │     holds your own words adds one rule: the smallest edit, in your voice
    │     ([the rule about your words](verbatim_rule)).
    │
    ●  claude answers, the tool checks
    │     Up to --tries times; each answer passes the pin checks.
    │
    ●  the map is saved
          Every stale mark goes, and the entry's own dependents, here and in
          every map with no code under it, are marked stale when a word
          changed. A repair that changed your words is named on the spot.

[ask_claude](ask_claude)(prompt, root)
    One call to claude with the letter; the answer is read as one JSON object.
    The letter goes in through the pipe, not on the command line, so a long one
    is never cut short. The call runs in the project root, so claude can open the
    files the letter names. A failed call stops the run.
